summary: Outpost Commander is a turn-based outpost sim for the junior and intermediate Space Apps audience. Each turn is one sol. Players spend a 12-tonne cargo budget on solar arrays, a fission reactor, batteries, a greenhouse, a water extractor, an oxygen generator, food, spares, and regolith shielding, then place them on an 8×8 map. Position matters: a reactor within three tiles of the habitat adds dose, and a greenhouse beside the habitat reuses grey water.
details:
Outpost Commander is a browser game where a player keeps four astronauts alive for one rotation on Mars (Jezero) or the Moon (south pole). Each turn is one sol. The player spends a fixed 12-tonne cargo budget on solar arrays, a fission reactor, batteries, a greenhouse, a water extractor, an oxygen generator, food stores, spares, and regolith shielding, then places those modules on an 8×8 map. Where a module sits changes the outcome: a reactor within three tiles of the habitat adds radiation dose, and a greenhouse beside the habitat reuses grey water. Life support already draws 3 kW. If power runs short, the greenhouse, water extractor, and oxygen generator shut down in that order. Dust storms cut Mars solar power to about 15 percent. A lunar night lasts 14 sols and shuts solar off completely. Story events, equipment failures, and four crew roles (morale, repair, healing, greenhouse yield) force a choice each day. The same classroom seed produces the same storms for every player. At the end, the debrief names the NASA project that works the problem that ended the rotation, such as Fission Surface Power, MOXIE, VIPER, Veggie, or MSL RAD. Two people can compete by playing the same seed and pasting a challenge code onto each other’s title screen. Highest XP on that seed wins.

The benefit is that mass, power, and siting become visible instead of staying inside a worksheet. Cadet mode (about ages 10–14) runs 60 sols with hints, extra supplies, and automatic repairs. Commander mode runs 120 sols and adds a heating load. XP is a rating of the plan: good siting can earn points, and blackouts, empty tanks, and a reactor parked too close lose points. Surviving is not enough. Many layouts can keep the crew alive. The ranking asks who planned more carefully.

The intended impact is a free classroom activity. Students compare decisions rather than luck, then leave the game with a real NASA link for the failure or success they just saw. No account and no install are required. Opening one HTML file is enough.

The game is a single HTML file with CSS and JavaScript, plus a folder of PNG illustrations. There is no framework and no server. Numbers come from published NASA figures: about 0.84 kg of oxygen and 1.8 kg of food per person per sol, about 3.5 kg of water with roughly 90 percent recovery while the pumps have power, about 0.7 mSv/sol on Mars and 1.3 mSv/sol at the lunar south pole, and a 600 mSv career limit. The illustrations were made with generative image tools. The 30-second demo uses a Mac system voice and on-screen English captions. The background music is generated in the page with the Web Audio API, so the project still hosts as static files on GitHub.

The creative part is that the engineering trade-off is a placement puzzle. Cable mass, radiation, grey water, dust, and lunar night are all positions and timing on the same map, not separate menus. A shared seed turns that into a fair contest: same sky, different plan.

The design holds two audiences at once, so Cadet and Commander share the same rules and change the length, the hints, and the heating load. It uses real consumption rates without adding a full life-support simulation. It keeps the debrief, because that is where the game connects to NASA. It stays in one file so a team can host it on GitHub Pages. It also treats “many crews can survive” as the start of the scoring problem, not the end of it.
